name: E-commerce platforms
one_line: The software that lets anyone run an online store, from a one-person shop to a global brand, without building the checkout themselves.
sells: Hosted or self-hosted store software: product pages, cart, checkout and payments, plus an app ecosystem, sold by subscription and by taking a cut of sales
customers: Businesses and individuals who sell online, from solo sellers to large brands
suppliers: Cloud hosting and compute, card networks and payment processors, logistics and fulfillment, and the app and theme developers who extend the platforms

revenue.metric: e-commerce platform revenue, anchored on Shopify's FY2025 total revenue (the dominant monetized platform)
revenue.note: No clean whole-industry revenue figure exists because the players monetize differently: Shopify earns $11.56B (+30%) on $378B of GMV from subscriptions plus a cut of payments, while WooCommerce leads by store count but is free open-source software (it earns through hosting, payments and plugins, not licenses). Wix, Squarespace, Adobe Commerce and BigCommerce add a few billion more. Shopify's revenue is used as the anchor; the full market is somewhat larger.

structure.why: Two platforms take roughly 69% of named-platform usage, but they are opposite models: WooCommerce (open-source, self-hosted, free) wins the long tail of small stores by raw count, while Shopify (managed SaaS) leads the larger, higher-traffic stores and dominates revenue and GMV. Wix, Squarespace and a tail of regional and enterprise platforms fill the rest.
structure.hhi_note: Sum of squared named-platform shares for the listed players (HTTP Archive, Oct 2026); a lower bound since the listed platforms cover ~93% of the named-platform market.

econ: A platform business with network effects and high switching costs: a store accumulates products, themes, apps and customer data that are painful to move, so merchants stay. The market splits on business model: free, self-hosted open-source software (WooCommerce) wins the long tail of small stores by count, while managed SaaS (Shopify) wins the larger stores and earns far more by taking a cut of payments as sales grow. It is a 'picks and shovels' trade: the platform profits from merchants' sales without having to pick which store wins.

Listed platforms cover ~93% of named-platform usage; the map draws the remainder as an 'All others' block.
